t: Maximum Number of Operations With the Same Score II — Interval DP
o: Repeatedly delete either the first two, last two, or outer two elements; every deletion scores the sum of the two removed values. All operations must share one score, and we maximize the operation count. Crucially, the very first operation fixes the score to one of three values: nums[0]+nums[1], nums[n-2]+nums[n-1], or nums[0]+nums[n-1]. Once the target score t is fixed, the process on the remaining window [l, r] is independent of history, so we can ask: what is the maximum number of deletions with sum t from interval [l, r]? Example 1 fixes t = 5 and achieves 3 deletions.
k: Only three candidate scores exist, determined by the first move.
For a fixed score, subproblems are intervals [l, r] with O(1) transitions — classic interval DP.
Answer = max over the three candidate scores of dp[0][n-1].

a.n: Approach 1: Interval DP per Candidate Score
a.i: Define dp[l][r] = max operations deleting pairs summing to t from nums[l..r]. From state (l, r) we may take the left pair, right pair, or outer pair, each valid only if its sum equals t, yielding 1 + dp of the shrunken interval. Fill by increasing interval length; run this once per candidate score and take the best.
s: For each candidate t in {nums[0]+nums[1], nums[n-2]+nums[n-1], nums[0]+nums[n-1]}:
Iterate l from n-2 down to 0, r from l+1 to n-1.
dp[l][r] = max of (1+dp[l+2][r]) if nums[l]+nums[l+1]==t, (1+dp[l][r-2]) if nums[r-1]+nums[r]==t, (1+dp[l+1][r-1]) if nums[l]+nums[r]==t, treating empty/invalid intervals as 0.
Return the maximum dp[0][n-1] across the three targets.
a.t: O(n²) per target, O(3n²) total — each interval filled once with O(1) transitions; n ≤ 2000 makes ~12M operations feasible.
a.sp: O(n²) — the DP table (reused across targets in compiled languages).

w: Always derive the three candidate scores from the first move — missing the outer-pair candidate is the classic mistake. Watch interval-shrink bounds (e.g., l+2 > r means the pair empties the array and contributes exactly 1). A follow-up might ask for the score itself or the actual sequence; store parent pointers in the DP.
